result:
There's a hum underneath everything.

It's not loud. You have to listen for it. It's the fridge at 2 a.m., it's the rain against a window you forgot to close all the way, it's the soft sigh your computer makes when it's been on too long. It's the sound of the world continuing while you're not paying attention.

I think about that a lot — how much of the world happens when we're not looking.

We talk about big moments. Graduations, heartbreaks, promotions, moves across the country. We archive those. We take photos. But life isn't really made of big moments. It's made of the thousands of tiny, unrecorded ones in between.

It's made of the way your friend always takes the ice out of their drink before they sip it. The exact way light hits your kitchen floor at 4:37 p.m. in October. The specific weight of your keys in your pocket. The joke you forgot to tell someone and then carried with you for three days.

None of that will ever make it into your biography. And yet, that's the texture of being alive.

I think we got it backwards. We think meaning is something you find, like a coin on the beach. But maybe meaning is something you *do* — something you apply, like a coat of paint. You take an ordinary Tuesday, with bad coffee and traffic and an email you didn't want to answer, and you decide to pay attention to it. Suddenly it's not ordinary anymore.

Attention is the real magic trick.

A few years ago, scientists found that even trees talk to each other. Through underground fungal networks, they share nutrients, warn each other about insects, even feed their young. They call it the Wood Wide Web. An old tree stump, felled years ago, will sometimes stay alive because the trees around it keep feeding it through its roots.

No one claps for that. No headlines. It just happens, quietly, in the dark soil.

People are like that too.

Someone remembers how you take your coffee after meeting you once. Someone lets you merge in traffic when you're running late. Someone saves a meme because it reminded them of you. Small, almost invisible acts of keeping each other alive.

We live in a world that is obsessed with being loud and fast and new. But the most important things are still slow and quiet and old.

Things like:
Waiting for bread to rise.
Writing something by hand and crossing it out.
Falling asleep on the couch and waking up with a blanket someone put over you.
Boredom. Real, stretching, phone-down boredom that finally forces your brain to make something weird and wonderful.

Maybe the point was never to be impressive. Maybe the point is to be *present*.

You don't have to become someone else to have a meaningful life. You just have to notice the one you already have.

So if no one has told you recently — the hum is still there. The world is still quietly, stubbornly continuing. And you are still part of it, whether you feel big today or small today.

That is enough. That has always been enough.

---

If you want, tell me a word — any word — and I'll write you a whole world around it.
